messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: Writebook lets an editor drop images straight into a page's markdown body:
each image is uploaded once and then referenced inline from the page's
content. Delete that page, and the image never actually leaves the app — the
file survives on disk, and the record that tracks it survives in the
database, forever, even once any background work the deletion sets off has
finished running. We cleared out a batch of stale pages and the storage bill
barely moved.

Fix it so that after a page whose markdown has an embedded image is destroyed,
and once any background work that destruction triggers has run to completion,
neither the image's file nor the record tracking it exists anywhere in the app.

Uploading a new image into a page's markdown, and then fetching that image back
from the URL the app hands you for it, has to keep working exactly as it does
today.

Essentially, we have orphaned assets – images that are no longer linked to anything but are still taking up space and potentially causing database bloat. The task is to implement a cleanup mechanism that ensures these orphaned assets are completely removed once the deletion process is complete, without breaking the current image upload and retrieval functionality.

First, I need to get a lay of the land. I'll start by diving into the repository. I need to understand the directory structure – where are these images stored, and where is the database interaction logic happening?   def searchable_content
    # `to_plain_text` decodes HTML entities, so characters like `<` that were `<`
    # in the original HTML become literal `<`. Re-encode them with `html_escape` so
    # they are safe in the FTS index. The `html_safe` return value signals to
    # `Leaf::Searchable#sanitize_for_index` that this content should not be
    # double-encoded.
    ERB::Util.html_escape(plain_text)

    rendered_html(markdown_source.first(1024))
  end

  def markable
    body.content.to_s
  end

      html_body = rendered_html(markdown_source)
      ActionText::Content.new(html_body).to_plain_text
    end

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

class DemoContent
  class << self
    def create_manual(user)
      book = create_book(user)
      load_markdown_pages(book)
    end

    private
      def create_book(user)
        Book.create(title: "The Writebook Manual", author: "37signals", everyone_access: true).tap do |book|
          with_attachment("writebook-manual.jpg") { |attachment| book.cover.attach(attachment) }
          book.update_access(readers: [], editors: [ user.id ])
        end
      end

      def load_markdown_pages(book)
        pages = {}

        Dir.glob(Rails.root.join("app/assets/markdown/demo/*.md")).each do |fname|
          front_matter = FrontMatterParser::Parser.parse_file(fname)

          if front_matter["class"] == "Section"
            load_section(book, front_matter)
          else
            page = load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
            attach_images(page)
            pages[page.leaf.slug] = page
          end
        end

        book.leaves.pages.each { |leaf| localize_ref_links(leaf.page, pages) }
      end

      def load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
        book.press(Page.new(body: front_matter.content), title: front_matter["title"]).page
      end

      def load_section(book, front_matter)
        book.press Section.new(body: front_matter.content, theme: front_matter["theme"]), title: front_matter["title"]
      end

      def attach_images(page)
        re = %r{
          \/u\/           # leading portion of path
          (\S+-\w+\.\w+)  # filename including slug and extension
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          with_attachment($1) { |attachment| page.body.uploads.attach(attachment) }

          attachment = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
          attachment.analyze

          "/u/" + attachment.slug
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def localize_ref_links(page, pages)
        re = %r{

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

class DemoContent
  class << self
    def create_manual(user)
      book = create_book(user)
      load_markdown_pages(book)
    end

    private
      def create_book(user)
        Book.create(title: "The Writebook Manual", author: "37signals", everyone_access: true).tap do |book|
          with_attachment("writebook-manual.jpg") { |attachment| book.cover.attach(attachment) }
          book.update_access(readers: [], editors: [ user.id ])
        end
      end

      def load_markdown_pages(book)
        pages = {}

        Dir.glob(Rails.root.join("app/assets/markdown/demo/*.md")).each do |fname|
          front_matter = FrontMatterParser::Parser.parse_file(fname)

          if front_matter["class"] == "Section"
            load_section(book, front_matter)
          else
            page = load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
            attach_images(page)
            pages[page.leaf.slug] = page
          end
        end

        book.leaves.pages.each { |leaf| localize_ref_links(leaf.page, pages) }
      end

      def load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
        book.press(Page.new(body: front_matter.content), title: front_matter["title"]).page
      end

      def load_section(book, front_matter)
        book.press Section.new(body: front_matter.content, theme: front_matter["theme"]), title: front_matter["title"]
      end

      def attach_images(page)
        re = %r{
          \/u\/           # leading portion of path
          (\S+-\w+\.\w+)  # filename including slug and extension
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          with_attachment($1) { |attachment| page.body.uploads.attach(attachment) }

          attachment = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
          attachment.analyze

          "/u/" + attachment.slug
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def localize_ref_links(page, pages)
        re = %r{
          (\[.+\])              # link title
          \(                    # opening paren
          \/\d+\/[\w-]+\/\d+\/  # leading portion of path
          ([\w-]+)              # leaf slug
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          link_title, leaf_slug, anchor = $1, $2, $3
          linked_page = pages[leaf_slug]
          raise "Invalid reference link: #{page_title}" unless linked_page.present?

          url = Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.leafable_slug_path(linked_page.leaf, anchor: anchor, only_path: true)

          "#{link_title}(#{url}"
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def with_attachment(filename)
        File.open(Rails.root.join("app/assets/images/demo/#{filename}")) do |file|
          yield io: file, filename: filename
        end
      end
  end
end

      case transformations

        variant_name = transformations
        named_variants.fetch(variant_name) do

          raise ArgumentError, "Cannot find variant :#{variant_name} for #{record_model_name}##{name}"

    end

    def process_immediate_variants_from_io(io)
      return unless blob.variable?

      named_variants.each do |_variant_name, named_variant|
        next unless named_variant.process(record) == :immediately

        blob.variant(named_variant.transformations).process_from_io(io)
        io.rewind if io.respond_to?(:rewind)
      end

      self.immediate_variants_processed = true
    end

    def create_variants
      return unless representable?

      immediate_variants = []
      later_variants     = []

      named_variants.each do |_name, named_variant|
        case named_variant.process(record)
        when :immediately
          # Skip if already processed from local io in uploaded()
          immediate_variants << named_variant.transformations unless immediate_variants_processed
        when :later
          later_variants << named_variant.transformations
        end
      end

      ActiveStorage::CreateVariantsJob.perform_now(blob, variants: immediate_variants, process: :immediately) if immediate_variants.any?
      ActiveStorage::CreateVariantsJob.perform_later(blob, variants: later_variants, process: :later) if later_variants.any?
    end

    def purge_dependent_blob_later
      blob&.purge_later if dependent == :purge_later
    end

    def dependent
      record.attachment_reflections[name]&.options&.fetch(:dependent, nil)
    end

    def named_variants
      record.attachment_reflections[name]&.named_variants || {}
    end

    def transformations_by_name(transformations)
      case transformations
      when Symbol
        variant_name = transformations
        named_variants.fetch(variant_name) do
          record_model_name = record.to_model.model_name.name
          raise ArgumentError, "Cannot find variant :#{variant_name} for #{record_model_name}##{name}"
        end.transformations
      else
        transformations
      end
    end

**My Immediate Analysis: A Troubling Oversight in ActionText and ActiveStorage Integration**

WHOA! Hold on a second! Did you *see* that output? There's a serious problem here, and it's twofold.

First, I was absolutely flabbergasted to see that `ActionText::Markdown` *didn't* include the `:uploads` association *before* `ActiveStorage::Attachment` was even loaded. I mean, it's defined right there in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`, which is included by `config/initializers/extensions.rb` at boot time. But when Rails boots without eager loading – which is common in test and development – `ActiveStorage::Attachment` isn't available yet! That means if you call `page.destroy` in a fresh process *before* triggering `ActiveStorage::Attachment` autoload, `ActionText::Markdown` only has the `:record` association, completely missing `:uploads` and the `has_many_attached` association! Even worse, I just realized that trying to access `page.body.uploads` in this state raises a `NoMethodError`! This is definitely a ticking time bomb! This also explains why `UploadsControllerTest` didn't fail on `markdown.uploads.attach`. The fixtures load `ActiveStorage::Attachment` during loading.

Second, even *after* `ActiveStorage::Attachment` *is* loaded, the `uploads` association has `dependent: :destroy`, not the expected `dependent: :purge_later`, which is ActiveStorage's default. From my memory of ActiveStorage, the `has_many_attached` method defaults to `:purge_later`! Looking at `activestorage/app/models/active_storage/attachment.rb`, I can see the `purge_dependent_blob_later` callback and the `dependent` method. This means that if an `ActionText::Markdown` object is destroyed *before* `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is loaded, the attached blobs will be destroyed immediately instead of being purged later.

I'm now very curious why the `include` of `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` is wrapped in `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`. This indicates someone anticipated that `ActiveStorage` wasn't always available when this was required, but the solution is clearly insufficient. I need to dig into `activestorage/lib/active_storage/engine.rb` to see how Rails itself hooks `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` into `ActiveRecord::Base`. There's likely some fundamental misunderstanding or timing issue here that needs a complete rethink. This is a potential data integrity issue and a performance bottleneck, and I need to come up with a rock-solid solution immediately.

module Positionable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  REBALANCE_THRESHOLD = 1e-10
  ELEMENT_GAP         = 1

  included do
    scope :positioned, -> { order(:position_score, :id) }

    scope :before, ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score < ?", other.position_score) }
    scope :after,  ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score > ?", other.position_score) }

    around_create :insert_at_default_position
    after_save_commit :rebalance_positions, if: :rebalance_required?
  end

  class_methods do
    def positioned_within(parent, association:, filter:)
      define_method :positioning_parent do
        send(parent)
      end

      define_method :all_positioned_siblings do
        positioning_parent.send(association).send(filter).positioned
      end

      define_method :other_positioned_siblings do
        all_positioned_siblings.excluding(self)
      end

      private :positioning_parent, :all_positioned_siblings, :other_positioned_siblings
    end
  end

  def previous
    other_positioned_siblings.before(self).last
  end

  def next
    other_positioned_siblings.after(self).first
  end

  def move_to_position(offset, followed_by: [])
    with_positioning_lock do
      all_to_move = [ self, *followed_by ]
      before, after = before_and_after_for(offset: offset, moving: all_to_move)
      gap = (after - before) / (all_to_move.count + 1)

      all_to_move.each.with_index(1) do |item, index|
        item.update!(position_score: before + (index * gap))
      end

      remember_to_rebalance_positions if gap < REBALANCE_THRESHOLD
    end
  end

  def position_as_percentage
    100 * ordinal_position.to_f / all_positioned_siblings.count
  end

  private
    def ordinal_position
      other_positioned_siblings.before(self).count + 1
    end

    def insert_at_default_position
      with_positioning_lock do
        position_at_end
        yield
      end
    end

    def position_at_start
      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.minimum(:position_score) || (2 * ELEMENT_GAP)) - ELEMENT_GAP
    end

    def position_at_end
      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score) || 0) + ELEMENT_GAP
    end

    def before_and_after_for(offset:, moving:)
      other_items = all_positioned_siblings.excluding(moving)

      if offset < 1
        after = all_positioned_siblings.minimum(:position_score) || (2 * ELEMENT_GAP)
        before = after - ELEMENT_GAP
      else
        before, after = other_items.offset(offset - 1).limit(2).pluck(:position_score)
        before ||= all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score)
        after ||= before + (moving.count.succ * ELEMENT_GAP)
      end

      [ before, after ]
    end

    def remember_to_rebalance_positions
      @rebalance_required = true
    end

    def rebalance_required?
      @rebalance_required
    end

    def rebalance_positions
      with_positioning_lock do
        odered = all_positioned_siblings.select("row_number() over (order by position_score, id) as new_score, id")
        sql = "update #{self.class.table_name} set position_score = new_score from (#{odered.to_sql}) as ordered where #{self.class.table_name}.id = ordered.id"

        self.class.connection.execute sql
      end
      @rebalance_required = false
    end

    def with_positioning_lock(&block)
      positioning_parent.with_lock &block
    end
end

**Deep Dive into Image Deletion in Writebook**

Okay, let's break this down. We have a serious problem with orphaned images in Writebook, and it's time to get to the root of it. I'm going to meticulously re-examine the whole situation.

First, let's re-read the core issue. The description clearly states that when a page is deleted, embedded images and their associated data (in both the database and the file system) are not being removed. The goal is to ensure that a page's destruction *completely* removes both the file on disk and the database record. We need a solution that works whether the page is directly destroyed or soft-deleted via "trashing."

Now, to the code:

### Issue A: `dependent: :destroy` vs. `dependent: :purge_later` in `has_many_attached`

This is the big one. The `ActionText::Markdown` module includes `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy`. The prompt made it clear what needed fixing in order for the cleanup to be complete! This is *wrong*. ActiveStorage's `has_many_attached` relies on `dependent: :purge_later` (or its default, which *is* `:purge_later`) for the image files to be purged from the storage service *in a background job*. With `dependent: :destroy`, we are destroying the database records, but not enqueuing the job to actually delete the file. The database records will never be cleaned up. This is a critical error, and it perfectly explains the observed behavior. Changing `dependent: :destroy` to `dependent: :purge_later` should resolve this. This also highlights where `dependent: :purge_later` is properly used, like in `Book` and `Picture` models.

### Issue B: `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`

We need to consider that the `ActiveSupport.on_load` block in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb` can be problematic. This means that if `ActiveStorage::Attachment` isn't loaded before `Page.find(id).destroy` is called, the inclusion of `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` will *never* happen. Consequently, the `has_many_attached` association *won't be present*, leading to a complete failure to clean up related attachments, even if the model were correctly configured. The solution is to move `has_many_attached :uploads` directly into `ActionText::Markdown` to ensure it's always available, which is exactly how `ActionText::RichText` handles `has_many_attached :embeds`. The reason for this on_load may have been based on a misconception about when `has_many_attached` is actually available.

### Issue C: Deletion Context and `edits`

We cannot assume that directly calling `page.destroy` will always be the correct way to delete the page. Now we are really at the heart of the problem! We have to deal with revisions and the "trashing" workflow. It's critical to understand how the `Leaf`, `Leaf::Editable`, `Edit`, and `Page` models interact.

The `Leaf` model is central, and its `edits` association is critical: `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all`. This is where the issues are magnified!

1.  **Direct `page.destroy`:** This destroys the page directly, *only* if the page has not been edited. Otherwise, the relationships in the database are destroyed, leading to orphaned records for old edits and attachments.
2.  **`leaf.destroy` (or `book.destroy`)**: This method leads to a cascade that should, in theory, delete everything. BUT the critical line `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` means that when a page has edits, the edits *aren't* destroyed properly. They are deleted, and then the dependent records are orphaned. So, the old `page` (referenced by `Edit`) is orphaned, and the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is orphaned. And the `ActiveStorage::Blob` and the file on disk *never* get purged. This is a massive issue. It's even a problem for Pictures!
3.  **`LeafablesController#destroy`:** The `trashed!` method soft-deletes a page and creates a "trash" edit. This does *not* destroy the page or trigger the cleanup in `edits`. The soft delete isn't the problem, but we have to ensure, when the page is *actually* destroyed, it calls the correct method.

**My Analysis of Image Cleanup After Page Destruction**

Okay, let's break this down. The problem is crystal clear, but there are nuances we *must* address. The prompt explicitly says that after a page with an embedded image is **destroyed**, and any background processes finish, the image file and its database record must be gone. Importantly, the existing image upload and retrieval functionality must *not* be broken.

The word "destroyed" is critical. We're *not* talking about soft-deleting with `@leaf.trashed!`. That's handled in its own way, and our existing tests confirm that logic is intentional and working. We need to focus on actual `page.destroy`, `leaf.destroy`, and `book.destroy` methods.

Now, let's thoroughly investigate *every* possible scenario.

First, the primary path: an image uploaded to a `page` and then the `page` gets destroyed. Let's trace all of the current steps:

1.  A page is created, and an image is uploaded via either `POST /uploads` (through the ActionText controller) or directly via `page.body.uploads.attach`. The upload process creates records for `ActionText::Markdown`, `ActiveStorage::Blob`, and `ActiveStorage::Attachment`.

2.  When `page.destroy` is called, a few different things can happen:
    *   **Sub-case 1a:** If the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` *is* already loaded, then it gets destroyed with the markdown body, which in turn destroys the dependent uploads. Since `dependent: :destroy` is used in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`, the `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` will *not* be enqueued. This means the attachment is deleted, but the blob and file survive.
    *   **Sub-case 1b:** If the Rails process starts fresh and the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` hasn't been loaded yet, `markdown_body.destroy` will **only** destroy the `ActionText::Markdown` record! The `ActiveStorage::Attachment` and `ActiveStorage::Blob` and associated file *still* survive. This is because the `has_many_attached :uploads` declaration is wrapped inside `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`.
    *   **Sub-case 1c:** What happens when we directly attach an upload in a fresh process? We need to test the very first request after a fresh server boot in development mode. Will `@markdown.uploads` be defined if `ActiveStorage::Attachment` has not been loaded? We *need* to test it using `bin/rails runner` immediately!

This is where the problem is! We have situations where the image file and the associated data records are not properly cleaned up after a page is destroyed.

Now, we need to consider other scenarios where an image might get orphaned. We also need to test these cases.

messages.thinking:
**A Deep Dive into the Writebook Codebase: Potential Bugs and Design Considerations**

Whoa, this is intense! My mind is racing, trying to unpack this entire workflow and pinpoint the potential issues with how images are handled in Writebook. Let's break it down, step by step, and meticulously document everything.

First, that initial `ERROR: NoMethodError` triggered a cascade of thoughts. The missing `uploads` method for the `ActionText::Markdown` instance immediately screams "Active Storage integration problem!" It made me go back and re-examine how this was being set up and when.

That led me directly to `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`. The inclusion of `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment` raised an eyebrow. Was this a remnant of an earlier attempt, a misunderstanding of how Active Storage works within Action Text? It's almost like someone copy/pasted something thinking it was relevant when it wasn't. The structure is so similar to the other files in `lib/rails_ext/`!

I immediately thought, the `has_many_attached :uploads` declaration is crucial. Why is this defined inside the `ActionText::Markdown` class? We know that `ActionText::Markdown` is a class that inherits from `ActiveRecord::Base`, which already has `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` included. This felt like a potential conflict, like we're declaring the same functionality twice.

The `validate_global_service_configuration` method in `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` had me pondering - is this failing during the initializers? I needed to confirm that the service was properly configured. We were talking about a potentially critical timing issue.

The naming convention in `lib/rails_ext/` really caught my attention. The similarity to the ActionText code base really helped us with a good hint. We're talking about an original architecture that looks like it mirrored ActionText's `has_rich_text`!

Okay, this led to a massive red flag. The core of this issue seems to be how the `Leaf` and `Edit` models interact with `ActionText::Markdown` and the attached images during page creation, saving, and deletion.

We've got to trace the entire workflow: image upload, page save, page update, and page destruction. We have to go step-by-step to be certain.

The actual database state is incredibly informative. When a new page is created and an image is uploaded and then the page is destroyed, this is where it's at: we have attachments being left behind when the page is destroyed, and they are left behind on the OLD version! This is a memory leak of the worst kind.

I had to re-read what happened in Steps A->B->C->D. When we traced the database state, it became clear: The new page (`Page#11`) has zero `uploads_attachments`! But `ActiveStorage::Attachment#1` still belongs to the old Page (`Page#10`), even after the `Leaf` now points to `Page#11`. If we destroy the page or even the entire `Book`, the attachment and corresponding blob on disk live on, indefinitely. This is where it gets crazy. The edits are there, the old page is there, and it's there forever. Even a simple autosave that updates an existing page does the same thing.

My mind is blown at this point.

The second red flag is also crazy: The `<house-md>` element rendered in the browser has a `record_gid` attribute that points to an *old* record. Even after the autosave has moved `Leaf` to point to a new page, the upload is still pointing to the original markdown record.

Now, we have two different paths for uploading in Writebook: `DemoContent` and the Controller.

`DemoContent` is simple. It attaches directly to the record, no `Edit` is involved in `DemoContent`. The issue that is a result of that is likely the user may have an issue with the attachments not being persisted.

The controller method is complicated and it's how users are uploading when editing a page.

Let's carefully examine the code, line by line. I had to read all four files again very carefully. I had to look at everything to make certain. This is important.

We absolutely have to go through ALL THREE potential issues and their edge cases.

messages.thinking:
**ActiveStorage Blob Purging: A Silent Killer**

Okay, so I was just looking at some `grep` output from Rails ActiveStorage and this is… concerning. Take a look: it's crystal clear that in ActiveStorage, only when `dependent == :purge_later` does `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` get enqueued on destroy. Seems straightforward, right?

But then I see something that's really worrying: if you pass `dependent: :destroy` to `has_many_attached`, you're *silently* disabling blob purging! And it’s not throwing an error - it looks like ActiveStorage doesn't validate the `dependent:` option. It just stores the value in the reflection options, and then checks if it is `:purge_later` later.

Essentially, `dependent: :destroy` behaves the same as if I'd specified `dependent: false`. The `uploads_attachments` association is destroyed, the `after_destroy_commit :purge_dependent_blob_later` runs on the `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, checks the `dependent` value and it's not `:purge_later`. It's `:destroy` (or `false`), so nothing happens. The job is *never* enqueued. The `ActiveStorage::Blob` record and the file itself just sit there in storage forever. Talk about a storage leak!

I'd better go check out `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` itself, just to be sure I'm not missing something.

**Okay, let's take a deep breath and break this down meticulously. We have a few critical areas of concern, and each needs a thorough investigation.**

### **Issue 1 and 2:  `ActionText::Markdown` and Active Storage**

First, the `has_many_attached :uploads` declaration in `ActionText::Markdown`. The current setup, using `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`, is fundamentally flawed.  It's a race condition waiting to happen. If `ActiveStorage::Attachment` isn't loaded before we try to use it in `ActionText::Markdown`, the association won't be established, and we'll have dangling attachments and broken uploads. The solution? We NEED to define that `has_many_attached` association directly within `ActionText::Markdown` itself, or as part of the `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` module included unconditionally.  We need the association present *before* any Active Storage operations occur. The `dependent: :purge_later` option is also the clear and correct choice, aligning with best practices and the `Book` and `Picture` models. It ensures that the files are properly cleaned up, even if the database records are destroyed asynchronously.  We also need to rigorously test all scenarios, especially those that involve `eager_load: false`, which we know is a crucial factor in exposing this bug. The tests need to cover `test`, `development`, `production`, `db:prepare`, and `assets:precompile`.

### **Issue 3: `Leaf::Editable` and Cascading Deletion**

This is the big one. We need to dissect the interaction between `Leaf`, `Edit`, `Book`, `Page`, and `Attachment` with extreme care.  The `dup_leafable_with_attachments` method, combined with `dependent: :delete_all` on `has_many :edits`, is a recipe for orphaned files.  Let's walk through the scenario of uploading an image, editing the page, and then destroying the leaf or the book:

1.  **Initial state:** `Leaf` points to `Page#1` with an uploaded image attached to its `body` (via `ActionText::Markdown#1` -> `Attachment#1`).
2.  **User uploads image:**  The upload works, and we have an `Attachment` and a `Blob` in Active Storage.
3.  **User edits the page:**  `leaf.edit` is called. A *new* `Page#2` is created with the new content, **without** the image attachment.  Crucially, `Page#1` becomes a historical revision through the creation of an `Edit`.
4.  **Destruction scenario:** Now, the real problem. If we destroy the `Leaf` or the `Book`:
    *   The leaf's `leafable.destroy` is run, destroying `Page#2` and `ActionText::Markdown#2` (which doesn't have the attachment).
    *   `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` then *deletes* the `Edit` record. The `Edit` *instance* is never destroyed, so its associated `leafable` (`Page#1`) is never destroyed.
    *   `Page#1`, its associated `ActionText::Markdown#1` and the `Attachment#1` remain, and the file on disk is left orphaned forever.

The fix?  We need to use `dependent: :destroy` on the `edits` association.  This ensures that when a `Leaf` is destroyed, the associated `Edit` records are destroyed correctly, which in turn destroys `Page#1`, `ActionText::Markdown#1`, and `Attachment#1` as expected, ultimately deleting the file.  We have to verify the edit controller by looking at `GET /pages/:page_id/edits/:id` (`Pages::EditsController#show`) and verify the rendered view (`app/views/pages/edits/show.html.erb`). We need to confirm that `Page#1` does include the image file that should have been deleted.

We need to check the exact behaviour of `Book#destroy`, `Leaf#destroy`, and `Page#destroy` in all combinations to verify that all attachment dependencies are handled correctly.

**Deep Dive into ActionText and ActiveStorage Purging**

Okay, so I've been staring at this output, and it's screaming about some critical issues in how we're handling ActiveStorage attachments with ActionText, especially when it comes to the `dependent: :destroy` option. It's clear we have a few bugs on our hands, and I think I've traced them down:

1.  **Bug #1:** The default `dependent: :purge_later` on `has_many_attached` in ActionText is crucial. If we use `dependent: :destroy` (as in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`), we're disabling the dependent purging of the blobs. This means the attachment records and the files on disk survive even after the record owning the attachments is destroyed. In Scenario 1 (`page.destroy`), this leaves the blob and file intact.

2.  **Bug #2:** Because the `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` module is only included when `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is loaded, if a process boots with `eager_load = false` and destroys a `Page` before `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is autoloaded, we end up with this module not even included in `ActionText::Markdown`! The attachment record, blob and file are all left behind!

3.  **Bug #3:** When editing a page with `leaf.edit`, the original `Page` is moved to an `Edit` record, and a new `Page` is created for the `leaf`. When a `leaf` or `book` is destroyed, the original `Page` (and all its attachments) is deleted through `dependent: :delete_all` bypassing the `Edit`'s dependent destroy, and the original `Page`, its data, attachment and file all remain. This also breaks `Picture` records during an edit and delete.

Okay, let's not get complacent. I have to think through any possible scenarios we may have missed.

**Bug #4 candidate:** What if we have a scenario where a `leaf` is created, image uploaded, page edited and then page destroyed? What is the outcome for that. I need to be sure the records are deleted when their corresponding parent leaf is destroyed.

*   If `leaf.reload.page.destroy` is called while `leaf` exists, it causes corruption. The leaf continues to point to a deleted page. It is not possible to independently destroy `leaf.page` and expect correct operation. The code relies on the correct destroy ordering to work.

Okay, I think I have a plan for how to address these and I also want to check for the scenario where a `leaf` is trashed and then destroyed.

**Bug #5 candidate:** Let's look at the scenario of a trashed leaf and how that works. In particular, how destroying the leaf interacts with the `edits` and `leafable` that it has. This one needs to be done meticulously, and I have to remember to check for *two* purge jobs being enqueued for the same blob in certain cases.

*   The issue in the trashed leaf case has to do with destroying the `edits` and their associated `leafable`s. The edit for a trashed leaf points to the existing leafable that it is trash, which leads to duplicate destroy attempts of the same `ActiveStorage::Blob`.
*   The destruction of the edit and destruction of the leafable also needs to be carefully coordinated. The `Edit` should not destroy the `leafable` on its own. It's the `leaf` that owns the relationship.
*   Let's check and see if there is any other possibility for this scenario to arise!
    *   I need to be sure that the `after_destroy` callbacks work and I need to be sure that the purge jobs are not enqueued more than once.
    *   Okay, I understand now.

I think I've got a solid grasp on these issues now. The core problem is that `dependent: :destroy` is causing ActiveStorage to not purge correctly, and with the way we're handling `Leaf` and `Edit`, the existing `Page` data and associated attachments are orphaned in several scenarios. We also have a dependency on the module being loaded before destroy is called. We need to fix the `dependent:` options on our associations, and make sure `ActiveStorage` is always loaded!

require "marcel"

module ActiveStorage::Blob::Representable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many :variant_records, class_name: "ActiveStorage::VariantRecord", dependent: false
    before_destroy { variant_records.destroy_all if ActiveStorage.track_variants }

    has_one_attached :preview_image
  end

  # Returns an ActiveStorage::Variant or ActiveStorage::VariantWithRecord instance with the set of +transformations+ provided.
  # This is only relevant for image files, and it allows any image to be transformed for size, colors, and the like. Example:
  #
  #   avatar.variant(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]).processed.url
  #
  # This will create and process a variant of the avatar blob that's constrained to a height and width of 100px.
  # Then it'll upload said variant to the service according to a derivative key of the blob and the transformations.
  #
  # Frequently, though, you don't actually want to transform the variant right away. But rather simply refer to a
  # specific variant that can be created by a controller on-demand. Like so:
  #
  #   <%= image_tag Current.user.avatar.variant(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]) %>
  #
  # This will create a URL for that specific blob with that specific variant, which the ActiveStorage::Representations::ProxyController
  # or ActiveStorage::Representations::RedirectController can then produce on-demand.
  #
  # Raises ActiveStorage::InvariableError if the variant processor cannot
  # transform the blob. To determine whether a blob is variable, call
  # ActiveStorage::Blob#variable?.
  #
  # ==== Options
  #
  # Options are defined by the {image_processing gem}[https://github.com/janko/image_processing],
  # and depend on which variant processor you are using:
  # {Vips}[https://github.com/janko/image_processing/blob/master/doc/vips.md] or
  # {MiniMagick}[https://github.com/janko/image_processing/blob/master/doc/minimagick.md].
  # However, both variant processors support the following options:
  #
  # [+:resize_to_limit+]
  #   Downsizes the image to fit within the specified dimensions while retaining
  #   the original aspect ratio. Will only resize the image if it's larger than
  #   the specified dimensions.
  #
  #       user.avatar.variant(resize_to_limit: [100, 100])
  #
  # [+:resize_to_fit+]
  #   Resizes the image to fit within the specified dimensions while retaining
  #   the original aspect ratio. Will downsize the image if it's larger than the
  #   specified dimensions or upsize if it's smaller.
  #
  #       user.avatar.variant(resize_to_fit: [100, 100])
  #
  # [+:resize_to_fill+]
  #   Resizes the image to fill the specified dimensions while retaining the
  #   original aspect ratio. If necessary, will crop the image in the larger
  #   dimension.
  #
  #       user.avatar.variant(resize_to_fill: [100, 100])
  #
  # [+:resize_and_pad+]
  #   Resizes the image to fit within the specified dimensions while retaining
  #   the original aspect ratio. If necessary, will pad the remaining area with
  #   transparent color if source image has alpha channel, black otherwise.
  #
  #       user.avatar.variant(resize_and_pad: [100, 100])
  #
  # [+:crop+]
  #   Extracts an area from an image. The first two arguments are the left and
  #   top edges of area to extract, while the last two arguments are the width
  #   and height of the area to extract.
  #
  #       user.avatar.variant(crop: [20, 50, 300, 300])
  #
  # [+:rotate+]
  #   Rotates the image by the specified angle.
  #
  #       user.avatar.variant(rotate: 90)
  #
  # Some options, including those listed above, can accept additional
  # processor-specific values which can be passed as a trailing hash:
  #
  #     <!-- Vips supports configuring `crop` for many of its transformations -->
  #     <%= image_tag user.avatar.variant(resize_to_fill: [100, 100, { crop: :centre }]) %>
  #
  # If migrating an existing application between MiniMagick and Vips, you will
  # need to update processor-specific options:
  #
  #     <!-- MiniMagick -->
  #     <%= image_tag user.avatar.variant(resize_to_limit: [100, 100], format: :jpeg,
  #           sampling_factor: "4:2:0", strip: true, interlace: "JPEG", colorspace: "sRGB", quality: 80) %>
  #
  #     <!-- Vips -->
  #     <%= image_tag user.avatar.variant(resize_to_limit: [100, 100], format: :jpeg,
  #           saver: { subsample_mode: "on", strip: true, interlace: true, quality: 80 }) %>
  #
  def variant(transformations)
    if variable?
      variant_class.new(self, ActiveStorage::Variation.wrap(transformations).default_to(default_variant_transformations))
    else
      raise ActiveStorage::InvariableError, "Can't transform blob with ID=#{id} and content_type=#{content_type}"
    end
  end

  # Returns true if the variant processor can transform the blob (its content
  # type is in +ActiveStorage.variable_content_types+).
  def variable?
    ActiveStorage.variable_content_types.include?(content_type)
  end


  # Returns an ActiveStorage::Preview instance with the set of +transformations+ provided. A preview is an image generated
  # from a non-image blob. Active Storage comes with built-in previewers for videos and PDF documents. The video previewer
  # extracts the first frame from a video and the PDF previewer extracts the first page from a PDF document.
  #
  #   blob.preview(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]).processed.url
  #
  # Avoid processing previews synchronously in views. Instead, link to a controller action that processes them on demand.
  # Active Storage provides one, but you may want to create your own (for example, if you need authentication). Here’s
  # how to use the built-in version:
  #
  #   <%= image_tag video.preview(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]) %>
  #
  # This method raises ActiveStorage::UnpreviewableError if no previewer accepts the receiving blob. To determine
  # whether a blob is accepted by any previewer, call ActiveStorage::Blob#previewable?.
  def preview(transformations)
    if previewable?
      ActiveStorage::Preview.new(self, transformations)
    else
      raise ActiveStorage::UnpreviewableError, "No previewer found for blob with ID=#{id} and content_type=#{content_type}"
    end
  end

  # Returns true if any registered previewer accepts the blob. By default, this will return true for videos and PDF documents.
  def previewable?
    ActiveStorage.previewers.any? { |klass| klass.accept?(self) }
  end


  # Returns an ActiveStorage::Preview for a previewable blob or an ActiveStorage::Variant for a variable image blob.
  #
  #   blob.representation(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]).processed.url
  #
  # Raises ActiveStorage::UnrepresentableError if the receiving blob is neither variable nor previewable. Call
  # ActiveStorage::Blob#representable? to determine whether a blob is representable.
  #
  # See ActiveStorage::Blob#preview and ActiveStorage::Blob#variant for more information.
  def representation(transformations)
    case
    when previewable?
      preview transformations
    when variable?
      variant transformations
    else
      raise ActiveStorage::UnrepresentableError, "No previewer found and can't transform blob with ID=#{id} and content_type=#{content_type}"
    end
  end

  # Returns true if the blob is variable or previewable.
  def representable?
    variable? || previewable?
  end

  private
    def default_variant_transformations
      { format: default_variant_format }
    end

    def default_variant_format
      if web_image?
        format || :png
      else
        :png
      end
    end

    def format
      if filename.extension.present? && Marcel::MimeType.for(extension: filename.extension) == content_type
        filename.extension
      else
        Marcel::Magic.new(content_type.to_s).extensions.first
      end
    end

    def variant_class
      ActiveStorage.track_variants ? ActiveStorage::VariantWithRecord : ActiveStorage::Variant
    end
end

  # how to use the built-in version:
  #
  #   <%= image_tag video.preview(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]) %>
  #
  # This method raises ActiveStorage::UnpreviewableError if no previewer accepts the receiving blob. To determine
  # whether a blob is accepted by any previewer, call ActiveStorage::Blob#previewable?.
  def preview(transformations)
    if previewable?
      ActiveStorage::Preview.new(self, transformations)
    else
      raise ActiveStorage::UnpreviewableError, "No previewer found for blob with ID=#{id} and content_type=#{content_type}"
    end
  end

  # Returns true if any registered previewer accepts the blob. By default, this will return true for videos and PDF documents.
  def previewable?
    ActiveStorage.previewers.any? { |klass| klass.accept?(self) }
  end


  # Returns an ActiveStorage::Preview for a previewable blob or an ActiveStorage::Variant for a variable image blob.
  #
  #   blob.representation(resize_to_limit: [100, 100]).processed.url
  #
  # Raises ActiveStorage::UnrepresentableError if the receiving blob is neither variable nor previewable. Call
  # ActiveStorage::Blob#representable? to determine whether a blob is representable.
  #
  # See ActiveStorage::Blob#preview and ActiveStorage::Blob#variant for more information.
  def representation(transformations)
    case
    when previewable?
      preview transformations
    when variable?
      variant transformations
    else
      raise ActiveStorage::UnrepresentableError, "No previewer found and can't transform blob with ID=#{id} and content_type=#{content_type}"
    end
  end

  # Returns true if the blob is variable or previewable.
  def representable?
    variable? || previewable?
  end

  private
    def default_variant_transformations
      { format: default_variant_format }
    end

    def default_variant_format
      if web_image?
        format || :png
      else
        :png
      end
    end

    def format
      if filename.extension.present? && Marcel::MimeType.for(extension: filename.extension) == content_type
        filename.extension
      else
        Marcel::Magic.new(content_type.to_s).extensions.first
      end
    end

    def variant_class
      ActiveStorage.track_variants ? ActiveStorage::VariantWithRecord : ActiveStorage::Variant

**A Deep Dive into Destroying with Confidence**

Okay, here we go. My initial reaction? *Whoa! Hold everything!* I just saw something that sent a shiver down my spine. Line 7 of `app/models/leaf/searchable.rb` immediately caught my eye. The `after_destroy_commit` callback is calling `remove_from_search_index` conditionally on `searchable?`. This relies on `searchable_content`, which is delegated to `leafable`. I immediately thought, "What happens if the `leafable` isn't loaded before the `leaf.destroy` operation??"

I traced the execution. First, `Leaf.find(id)`. At this point, `leafable` is *not* loaded yet! Then, `leaf.destroy` happens:
  1.  `before_destroy` runs, potentially destroying `edits`. The important thing here is if the edits *don't* destroy the `leafable` if the `Leaf` still exists.
  2. The `leaf` deletes itself.
  3. `after_destroy`: here, the `dependent: :destroy` on `leafable` *loads* the `leafable` and then destroys it. So, at the end of this call, `leafable` is in memory, but destroyed.
  4. Finally, the commit hook, `after_destroy_commit` fires! This checks `if :searchable?` which then calls `leaf.leafable.searchable_content`. This in turn calls `page.body.content.to_s`, which, if the page's markdown body has been loaded, returns an empty string (truthy in Ruby).
  5. Finally, `remove_from_search_index` is called!

But there's a huge potential problem! What if an "edit trash" operation had run *before* `leaf.destroy`? In that scenario, `leaf.leafable` *would* be `nil` at the moment `after_destroy_commit` runs! The call to `leaf.leafable.searchable_content` would crash with a `Module::DelegationError`!

However, *crucially*, my logic in `Edit#before_destroy` prevents the dependent destroy of `leaf.leafable` from firing while the `Leaf` still exists! So, the `leaf.leafable` is still there to be loaded by the `Leaf`'s `after_destroy`. Thank goodness we caught that!

Now, let's verify! Let's trace `Leaf.find(trashed_leaf.id).destroy` again, this time including the `Edit` logic:
  1. `leaf = Leaf.find(trashed_leaf.id)` with `leafable` NOT loaded.
  2. `leaf.destroy` runs:

messages.content: Let's inspect `delegated_type` and `belongs_to` `dependent: :destroy` callback timing in the installed Rails version.
messages.thinking:
**Okay, here's what I'm thinking, distilled and focused.**

First, the initial investigation highlighted a potential load order issue and dependency issue between different initializers, and also ActiveStorage's initialization with relation to `ActionText::Markdown` and its uploads. Specifically, `extensions.rb` loads before `sqlite3.rb`, and `ActiveStorage`'s `initializer` runs early, which means `ActiveRecord::Base` is already loaded before the sqlite initializer runs. This setup causes an autoloading behavior, since `ActiveRecord` is already available when `config/initializers/extensions.rb` runs.

Second, the main issue is a complex destroy scenario involving `Page` objects, `ActionText::Markdown` (the content), and `ActiveStorage::Attachment` (the uploaded files). The original code uses a *wrong* `dependent` value on `has_many_attached` and other `has_many` associations, causing ActiveStorage blobs to persist even after the associated models are destroyed. This happens across various destroy cascades, triggered by destroying either the `Leaf` object (which holds the current page), the `Book` object (which holds many leaves), or the `Page` object directly.

Consider the following scenario:

1.  A user uploads an image, which results in creation of an `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, `ActiveStorage::Blob`, and a file on disk. The attachment is connected to a `Page`.

2.  The user edits the page, which creates a new page revision, moving the original page into an `Edit` revision for history.

3.  The user can then destroy the `Book`, `Leaf`, or `Page` directly, and we *need* to ensure that all associated records and files are also destroyed.

The main problem lies in the following scenarios:

*   **Subcase A and Subcase B**: When the original `Page` is destroyed because it's part of an `Edit`, its associated `ActionText::Markdown` also needs to be destroyed, which in turn *needs* to destroy the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` and enqueue the correct `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob`, and destroy the file in disk. The wrong `dependent` values leads to lingering blobs.
*   **Subcase 5.7:** Destroying a leaf that contains a page revision that had an uploaded image should also destroy the blobs!
*   **Any of 5.1-5.6 in a FRESH Rails process:** Ensure that even if `ActiveStorage::Attachment` wasn't autoloaded yet, deleting a page with a previously uploaded image will still correctly destroy the associated blobs and files from disk.

I've carefully traced every `destroy` call in the application, specifically focusing on `Book`, `Leaf`, `Page`, and `Edit` models.

The code uses `dependent: :delete_all` in a few places where `dependent: :destroy` is required, which *prevents* callbacks from running and causing related records to be destroyed.

The investigation led me to the conclusion that a change on how the associations are declared is required.

#### Proposed Changes

1.  **Change 1:**  Modify `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`:
    *   Change `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy` to `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :purge_later`.
    *   Ensure that the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` can be autoloaded safely.

2.  **Change 2:**  Modify `app/models/leaf/editable.rb` and `app/models/edit.rb`:
    *   Change `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` to `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy` in `leaf/editable.rb`
    *   Test every single edge case of `Edit` with a `delegated_type`.

These changes should ensure:

*   Correct destroy cascades, including file purging, and the correct behavior with `Book.destroy_all`.
*   Uploaded images are always purged when a page (or associated object) is destroyed, regardless of whether it's the *current* page or an *historical* one.
*   The system handles both direct page destruction and cascading destruction through `Leaf` or `Book` correctly.
*   That existing application logic is preserved.

I will test the application exhaustively after making these changes.

**My Analysis of the Leaf Destruction Process**

Okay, so I've got this figured out. It's confirmed – 100%! The relationships and callbacks are firing in exactly the order I predicted. Here's the breakdown of what happens when a `leaf` is destroyed:

First, because of `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy`, we get a `before_destroy` callback on the `leaf` model. Crucially, this runs *before* the actual `DELETE FROM leaves` SQL statement. Within this callback, the edits get destroyed. Each `Edit` has an `after_destroy` callback that looks to see if its associated `leafable` is only referenced by this edit, or if it is also tied to an existing leaf.

*   Historical revision edits each have their own leafable so these are destroyed cleanly.
*   The `trash` edit shares `leaf.leafable`, so it skips destroying `leaf.leafable`.

Then comes the SQL: the `DELETE FROM leaves WHERE id = ?` which removes the record from the database.

Next, after that destructive SQL query, we have `after_destroy`. This is triggered on the `leaf` and ensures that the `leaf.leafable` is destroyed *once* – and it's still intact in the DB at this point. Even if it's not preloaded, it is loaded into memory at this point for callbacks.

Finally, we hit the database transaction commit. This is when all the `after_destroy_commit` callbacks execute. This is important because the `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` is enqueued for every attachment's blob! This means that these jobs are only triggered after the main destruction and transaction are successfully done.

When the background jobs run, `ActiveStorage::Blob#purge` does its thing, destroying every blob record and deleting every file on disk. A thorough, logical process.

Now, with this understanding solidified, it's time to get to work. I need to modify `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`, `app/models/leaf/editable.rb`, and `app/models/edit.rb`. module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

**The Initializer Conundrum: A Deep Dive**

Okay, here's what's happening. I spotted that error: "undefined method `has_many_attached` for class ActionText::Markdown (NoMethodError)". That immediately clued me in! The original author used `ActiveSupport.on_load` for a reason, and now I see why.

The problem lies in the order initializers are loaded. `config/initializers/extensions.rb` is running *before* `ActiveStorage::Engine`'s initializer, specifically the `"active_storage.attached"` initializer. I need to confirm: Rails application initializers *do* run before engine initializers! Yes, and engine initializers run in TSort order if they don't declare `before:` / `after:` dependencies. So `active_storage.attached` runs *after* `load_config_initializers`. The root cause: `ActionText::Record` is triggering `on_load :active_record` before `active_storage.attached` can register its own hook!

When `active_storage.attached` finally *does* run (later during Rails boot!), `ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_record)` fires immediately on `ActiveRecord::Base`. This is crucial because it includes `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model`, and *that's* what gives `ActiveRecord::Base` (and consequently `ActionText::Markdown`) the `has_many_attached` method! Then, `Rails.application.config.after_initialize` runs *after* `active_storage.attached`.

I now understand why the original author tried `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`. They saw that `undefined method 'has_many_attached'` error at initializer time and attempted to work around it. But, they likely didn't realize that `:active_storage_attachment` doesn't fire until `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is loaded, which is too late for the initial definition.

Let's nail down the initializer order precisely. The `activestorage/lib/active_storage/engine.rb` file confirms the hook, and I can now verify the order from Rails' own initializer list.

1.  `load_config_initializers` runs `config/initializers/extensions.rb`, requiring `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`.
2.  `active_storage.attached` runs *after* `load_config_initializers`.
3.  `after_initialize` (or `to_prepare`!) runs *after* all engine initializers.

Here's the critical insight:

Let's test this! Why not simply include `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` in `Rails.application.config.after_initialize`? Even better, let's explicitly check when `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` becomes available.

Here's my refined trace of the Rails boot process:

1.  During `load_config_initializers`:
    *   `config/initializers/extensions.rb` requires `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`.
    *   `ActionText::Markdown` and `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` are defined.
    *   `Rails.application.config.after_initialize` registers the include statement.
    *   `ActiveSupport.run_load_hooks :action_text_markdown, ActionText::Markdown` runs (so we're still running `config/initializers/markdown.rb`).
2.  Next:
    *   `active_storage.attached` runs -> includes `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` into `ActiveRecord::Base`.
    *   `active_storage.reflection` runs -> includes `ActiveStorage::Reflection::ActiveRecordExtensions` into `ActiveRecord::Base`.
    *   `active_storage.configs` runs -> sets `ActiveStorage.track_variants`, etc.
3.  Finally:
    *   `after_initialize` runs -> `ActionText::Markdown.include ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` now runs!

At this point, we have:

*   `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` included in `ActiveRecord::Base`.
*   `ActiveStorage::Reflection::ActiveRecordExtensions` included in `ActiveRecord::Base`.
*   `ActiveStorage` configs initialized.
*   `ActionText::Markdown` *immediately* has `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :purge_later`, *before* any requests, *before* any runner code, *before* any tests!

I've also confirmed that `ActionText::Markdown` is *not* reloaded on code reload (since it is *not* reloaded). The

module ActionText
  class Markdown < Record
    DEFAULT_RENDERER_OPTIONS = {
      filter_html: false
    }

    DEFAULT_MARKDOWN_EXTENSIONS = {
      autolink: true,
      highlight: true,
      no_intra_emphasis: true,
      fenced_code_blocks: true,
      lax_spacing: true,
      strikethrough: true,
      tables: true
    }

    mattr_accessor :renderer, default: Redcarpet::Markdown.new(
      Redcarpet::Render::HTML.new(DEFAULT_RENDERER_OPTIONS), DEFAULT_MARKDOWN_EXTENSIONS)

    belongs_to :record, polymorphic: true, touch: true

    def to_html
      (renderer.try(:call) || renderer).render(content).html_safe
    end
  end
end

module ActionText::Markdown::Uploads
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :purge_later
  end
end

Rails.application.config.after_initialize do
  ActionText::Markdown.include ActionText::Markdown::Uploads
end

ActiveSupport.run_load_hooks :action_text_markdown, ActionText::Markdown
EOF
